title: The Quiet Return of Tide Pooling
author: Mara Ellison
excerpt: A once-forgotten low-tide ritual is showing up again on beaches from Maine to Monterey — and it's teaching a generation raised on screens to look closely at something slow.
body:
There's a specific kind of quiet that settles over a beach an hour before low tide. The gulls thin out, the wind drops, and the water pulls back to reveal a world that was there the whole time, just underwater: anemones closed into fists, hermit crabs mid-argument over a shell, a sculpin freezing mid-dart under a rock ledge.

Tide pooling never really went away, but it's having a visible resurgence — local naturalist groups from Maine to Monterey report waitlists for their low-tide walks for the first time in a decade. Part of it is practical: tide charts are now a notification away, and a decent macro lens is built into every phone. But talk to the people leading these walks and they'll tell you it's less about the photos and more about the pace. You can't tide pool quickly. The pools reward the person willing to crouch for ten minutes and watch nothing happen, until something does.

If you want to try it yourself: check a tide chart for a minus tide (anything below 0.0 ft is ideal), wear shoes with real grip, and never turn over a rock without putting it back exactly as you found it. Whatever's living under there depends on staying wet and hidden.

title: What a Lighthouse Keeper Actually Does in 2026
author: Owen Reyes
excerpt: Most lights have been automated for decades, but a handful of keepers still live on the rocks. We asked one what the job looks like now.
body:
The light itself hasn't needed a human in over 40 years — a photocell switches it on at dusk, and the bulb change is a five-minute job maybe twice a year. So what does a modern lighthouse keeper actually do?

Mostly: maintenance, weather, and stories. The keepers who remain (fewer than a dozen paid positions left in the US, split between historical societies and a couple of Coast Guard exceptions) spend their days on the unglamorous work of keeping a 19th-century structure from falling into the ocean it warns ships away from — repointing masonry, servicing the generator, logging conditions that still occasionally get radioed to passing vessels in fog.

The stories part is newer. Most active lighthouses now run a visitor program, and keepers have become de facto historians, giving tours to people who drove two hours to stand at the base of something that predates their grandparents. One keeper we spoke with put it simply: 'The light doesn't need me anymore. The story does.'

title: The Case for a Smaller Boat
author: Mara Ellison
excerpt: Everyone assumes bigger is the goal. The sailors and fishermen who've owned both tell a different story.
body:
Ask a marina full of boat owners what they'd change and a surprising number say the same thing: they'd go smaller. Not because they can't afford the upkeep on something bigger — though that's real too, a rule of thumb puts annual maintenance at 10% of a boat's value — but because a smaller boat gets used.

A 42-foot sailboat takes a full morning to prep, needs a slip that costs real money, and demands a crew for anything beyond a calm afternoon. A 16-foot skiff goes from driveway to water in fifteen minutes, singlehanded, on a whim after work. Over a season, the math on 'boat actually used' tends to favor the smaller hull by a wide margin.

This isn't an argument against ever owning something larger — a family that wants to live aboard for a summer has different needs entirely. It's an argument for buying for the trips you'll actually take on a Tuesday evening, not the two-week Bahamas trip you take once every three years.

title: Reading a Wave Forecast Like a Local
author: Priya Nair
excerpt: Swell height alone tells you almost nothing. Here's what surfers actually look at before paddling out.
body:
A forecast that says '4 feet' can mean anything from glassy and rideable to closed-out and dangerous, depending on three numbers most beginners skip past: period, direction, and wind.

Period (the seconds between wave crests) matters more than height. A 4-foot swell at 8 seconds is a weak, mushy wind-swell. The same 4 feet at 16 seconds is a long-period groundswell that will hit the sandbar with real power — often doubling in face height as it stands up. Direction decides which beaches even get the swell at all, since most coastlines only face a narrow window of open ocean. And wind is the tiebreaker: offshore wind (blowing from land to sea) grooms a wave into a clean face; onshore wind chops the same swell into mush within an hour.

Locals read all three together, then check one more thing that no app tracks well: the tide stage at the specific sandbar they're paddling out to, since the same swell can be unrideable at low tide and perfect two hours later.

title: The Unglamorous Economics of a Fishing Town
author: Owen Reyes
excerpt: Behind every postcard-pretty harbor is a supply chain running on thinner margins than most people assume.
body:
The harbor looks the same as it did fifty years ago — same weathered pilings, same gulls fighting over bait — but the economics underneath it have quietly changed. Fuel is the biggest line item now, often 30-40% of a trip's cost before a single fish is landed, which means a boat can come home with a full hold and still lose money if diesel spiked that week.

Most small operators have adapted by selling direct: a dock-side stand or a standing order with three restaurants beats waiting for a wholesale buyer whose price resets every morning based on that day's total catch across the whole coast. It's more paperwork and no guaranteed buyer, but it keeps a bigger share of each dollar with the person who caught the fish.

The towns that are thriving aren't the ones that caught the most — they're the ones that figured out how to sell what they caught for what it's actually worth.

title: A Short History of the Beach Umbrella
author: Priya Nair
excerpt: It took nearly a century to go from a parasol borrowed off the street to the wind-anchored tent-poles lining beaches today.
body:
The beach umbrella as we know it — a fabric canopy on a pole, driven into sand rather than held — is younger than most people assume. Through the early 1900s, beachgoers mostly used ordinary parasols meant for city streets, which is exactly as impractical in wind as it sounds. The pointed, sand-anchored spike design that solved this didn't become widespread until manufacturers started marketing purpose-built beach umbrellas in the 1950s, riding the same postwar leisure boom that gave us the aluminum beach chair.

Today's version has quietly gotten more engineered than it looks: the better ones use a vented canopy (a small hole or flap at the top) specifically to let wind pass through instead of catching the whole umbrella like a sail, which is the actual cause of most umbrella-related beach injuries — not the spike, the airborne canopy.

If you're shopping for one, the vent and a screw-anchor base (rather than a straight spike) are the two features actually worth paying more for.
